title: Design an ML-Driven Notification Targeting System
prompt: Design a system that decides which push/email notifications to send to each user, when to send them, and how often. It should use ML to predict engagement propensity, optimize send time, and avoid over-notifying users. Assume a large consumer app with many notification types competing for attention.
blurb: ML notification targeting: propensity scoring, send-time optimization, and fatigue/frequency capping without tanking long-term engagement.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (candidate notifications, propensity scoring, send-time, frequency capping, channel choice) from non-functional (throughput, freshness, respecting caps, long-term engagement).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about notification types, objective (opens vs long-term retention vs revenue), channels, volume, opt-outs/regulatory limits, real-time vs batch.

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Derives users × candidate notifications, scoring QPS/batch size, feature fetch volume, send throughput, storage for events and features.

rubric.label: Propensity / engagement model
rubric.description: Predicts P(engage | user, notification, context); features (user history, notification content, recency, context); ranking candidates; utility beyond click.

rubric.label: Send-time & fatigue optimization
rubric.description: Send-time optimization per user, frequency/fatigue capping, diminishing returns, avoiding annoyance-driven opt-outs and unsubscribes.

rubric.label: Feature pipeline & store
rubric.description: Online features (recent activity, last-notified, session state) + offline features (long-term engagement), freshness, training-serving parity.

rubric.label: Evaluation & long-term impact
rubric.description: Offline metrics (AUC/calibration) vs online A/B on the right objective (retention, opt-out rate, not just CTR), holdouts, guarding against short-term-click optimization, drift.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Candidate generation → propensity scoring → send-time + fatigue policy → channel delivery; async engagement logging → training + feature updates.

rubric.label: Scaling & reliability
rubric.description: Batch vs real-time scoring, delivery throughput, sharded feature store, backpressure, respecting caps under failures, dedup.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Send/open/opt-out metrics, per-notification-type performance, feature freshness, cap adherence, model version tracking, drift.

rubric.label: Privacy & user trust
rubric.description: Consent/opt-outs, channel regulations, PII in content, avoiding manipulative patterns, respecting quiet hours.

functional_requirements: Generate candidate notifications per user (from many producers)
Score engagement propensity for each candidate
Choose whether to send, which channel, and when (send-time optimization)
Enforce frequency/fatigue caps across all notification types
Log engagement and unsubscribes for learning
nonfunctional_requirements: Handle large user base × many candidate notifications efficiently
Respect frequency caps and quiet hours reliably
Optimize long-term engagement, not just immediate opens
Reproducible decisions with logged features + model version
clarifying_questions: What notification types exist and who produces them?
What's the real objective — opens, sessions, retention, revenue?
Which channels (push, email, in-app) and any legal frequency limits?
How many users and candidate notifications per user per day?
Real-time triggers, scheduled batches, or both?
Do users have explicit preferences / quiet hours?
qualifying_questions: Is over-notification currently causing opt-outs (fatigue a known problem)?
One global frequency cap or per-channel/per-type?
Do we need per-user send-time or is a global best-time acceptable?

estimations.scale: 100M users × ~10 candidate notifications/day = ~1B scoring events/day → mostly batch, with real-time for triggered events
estimations.scoring: Batch score overnight/hourly; real-time path for time-sensitive triggers at moderate QPS
estimations.feature_fetch: Per-user features (history, last-notified, context) from an online store; precompute heavy features offline
estimations.delivery: Send throughput must handle bursts (e.g. breaking events) with rate limiting to channels
estimations.storage: Engagement events + features: many TB; retain history for training + long-term metrics

data_model: sends(user_id, notif_id, channel, sent_at, score, model_version)
api_design: POST /v1/candidates { user_id, notifications[] } → enqueued for scoring
policy decide(user_id, scored_candidates[]) → { send?, channel, at } respecting caps
POST /v1/engagement { user_id, notif_id, action } → async into log
reference.high_level_design: Notification producers emit candidates per user into an aggregation layer that dedups and collects them. A propensity model scores P(engage) for each candidate using user features (recent + long-term activity, last-notified recency), notification content features, and context. A send-time model predicts each user's likely-active windows. A policy engine then decides what to actually send: it ranks candidates by expected utility, applies frequency/fatigue caps and quiet hours across all types, and schedules delivery at the optimized time through the appropriate channel. Most scoring runs in batch (hourly/nightly) with a real-time path for time-sensitive triggers. Engagement — opens, dismisses, and crucially unsubscribes — streams into a log that updates features and feeds retraining. Models are evaluated online with A/B tests and long-term holdouts on retention and opt-out rate, not just CTR.

deep_dives.probe: You predict P(open). But maximizing opens can train the model to spam. How do you define utility so you value long-term engagement and penalize opt-outs, not just the immediate click?
How do you learn each user's best send time? What features, and how do you handle users with little history (cold start)?
Multiple producers all want to notify the same user. How does the policy engine arbitrate, enforce a global fatigue cap, and model diminishing returns / annoyance?
A model that raised CTR this week could be hurting retention via opt-outs. How do you evaluate — long-term holdouts, guardrail metrics — to avoid short-term-metric traps?
How do you ensure last-notified / recency features at training time match serving? Point-in-time correctness matters because these change fast.
A brand-new user or a brand-new notification type has no engagement history. How do you score and send responsibly, and explore without annoying?
A user just opted out or changed preferences, or just took an action in-app. How does that state change reach the scoring path quickly so you don't send a notification you shouldn't?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions feature store or features or last-notified
followup_bank.question: When a user's state changes in the source system (opt-out, preference change, just-completed action), how does that propagate into the online feature store so scoring sees it fast — CDC/change-stream vs periodic recompute? What staleness is safe?

You cache per-user scores or features between batches — what's the eviction/TTL, and when the user's state changes how do you invalidate stale-after-change entries so you don't send based on outdated data?
How do you roll out a new model and prove it helps long-term engagement, not just this week's CTR — A/B plus long-term holdout on which metrics?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions cap or frequency or fatigue
followup_bank.question: How does the policy engine enforce a global cap across all producers and model diminishing returns, and what happens on a breaking-event burst?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions CTR or opens or engagement
followup_bank.question: Why is optimizing opens alone risky, and how do you incorporate opt-out/unsubscribe cost into the objective?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions cold start or new user
followup_bank.question: How do you score and send for users or notification types with no history, and how do you explore safely?

scaling: Batch scoring for the bulk; real-time path only for triggered/time-sensitive notifications
Sharded online feature store keyed by user
Rate-limited channel delivery with burst handling and dedup
Idempotent send + cap enforcement resilient to retries
bottlenecks: Feature freshness for fast-changing recency/last-notified signals
Delivery bursts on breaking events vs channel limits
Label sparsity for rare notification types
tradeoffs: Real-time scoring (fresh, costly) vs batch (cheap, staler)
Single utility model vs separate propensity + send-time + fatigue models
alternative_solutions: Bandit approach balancing exploration of send-time/content
Uplift modeling — send only when it changes behavior, not to already-active users
observability: Send/open/dismiss/opt-out rates by notification type + channel
Long-term engagement/retention dashboards and drift alerts
security: Respect consent, opt-outs, and channel regulations (e.g. quiet hours)
PII handling in notification content and logs
Access control on producer APIs to prevent spam
Rate limiting per user across all producers
reference.reference_answer: A strong mid-level answer separates candidate generation, propensity scoring, send-time optimization, and a fatigue/frequency-cap policy engine, and is explicit that the objective must be long-term engagement — penalizing opt-outs — not raw opens, because maximizing clicks trains the system to spam. It scores mostly in batch with a real-time path for time-sensitive triggers, fetching fast-changing recency/last-notified features from an online store and precomputing heavier features offline, with attention to training-serving parity on those volatile features. It arbitrates across competing producers under a global cap, handles cold start for new users/notification types, and evaluates models with online A/B plus long-term holdouts on retention and unsubscribe rate rather than short-term CTR. It keeps user state fresh (opt-outs and just-taken actions must reach scoring fast) and respects consent, quiet hours, and channel limits.

interviewer_notes: This is a mid-level question, so a solid structured answer (candidate generation → propensity → send-time → fatigue policy → delivery, with a feedback loop) earns a good score. The key thing to push, even at mid-level, is the objective: candidates who optimize P(open) without recognizing that it drives spam and opt-outs are missing the central insight — steer them to a utility that values long-term engagement and penalizes unsubscribes, and evaluate with long-term holdouts, not just weekly CTR. This is the evaluation/ml-specifics dimension. Probe fatigue/frequency capping across competing producers and send-time optimization concretely. When they place a feature store, hit the CDC/freshness probe: an opt-out or just-taken action must reach scoring fast. When they add a per-user score/feature cache between batches, probe eviction and stale-after-change. Cold start (new user / new notification type) is a good stretch probe. Don't expect the depth of the senior questions on stats or serving internals, but do expect awareness of the long-term-vs-short-term metric trap.
